TEXT:
F ormer Glencore coal executive-turn-real estate mogul Vaughan Blank and his wife Jacqueline have bought Woollahra’s historic Victorian Italianate villa – the Hughenden.

There is already talk of redevelopment plans for the 1356-square-metre site at the top of Queen Street once the sale settles, although Woollahra Council is yet to receive any applications.

Children’s author Susanne Gervay bought it as a fire-damaged wreck in 1992 for $1.71 million and restored it to create a 32-room hotel that was where Gretel Packer's former husband, spiritual advisor Shane Murray, retreated when their marriage hit the skids in 2007.

Built in 1878 for Dr Frederick Harrison Quaife, president of the British Medical Society, from 1913 it was the Riviere     College, before it became better known as a boarding house and later a guest house.

CELEBRITY HIDEAWAY FOR SALE

A modern Gold Coast haven which recently hosted a Hollywood star has entered the market, with $3.6 million hopes.

The Palm Springs-inspired home at 2234  Arnold Palmer Drive, Sanctuary Cove, is being sold by Graham and Linda Gordon, music agents and tour promoters.

While selling agent Alex Phillis of Ray White Runaway Bay wouldn’t name the Hollywood celeb who’s stayed, thanks to a non-disclosure agreement.

We’d hazard a guess it was perhaps a star of the Thor movie which was recently filmed in Brisbane.

The four-bedroom, five-bathroom property has north-facing views over the 15th hole of the exclusive Arnold Palmer golf course The Pines.

As well as the home’s single-floor layout and abundance of natural light, the agent said it’s the privacy and exclusivity of the property is what sets it apart.

“It’s a little world of its own,” Phillis says. "You look out at the greenery and the gold course and the kangaroos. RC

MICHAEL KOLLOSCHE

KOLLOSCHE PRESTIGE AGENTS

HOW

DID YOU GET INTO THE REAL ESTATE BUSINESS?

I started working with Ray White in Broadbeach as a receptionist before commencing sales a few years later. Things progressed and before I knew it I was the No. 1 international salesperson for the Ray White Network for a few consecutive years.

WHAT DO YOU LOVE ABOUT YOUR WORK?

I enjoy the interaction with buyers and sellers and seeing amazing homes, but my real passion is the negotiation, putting the deals together.

DESCRIBE THE PRESTIGE GOLD COAST MARKET TODAY?

The market is very buoyant. It sat in a lull for many years post GFC but it has turned and we are seeing strong consistent transactions and signs of capital appreciation as stock levels tighten up.

WHAT ARE THE CURRENT OPPORTUNITIES ?

Vendors have the opportunity to leverage off a diminishing supply to achieve strong sales prices and shouldn’t be in a rush to deal. Buyers are losing more leverage every day, unfortunately, and it would seem that if they don’t move soon, prices will keep moving upwards and it may cost them considerably in the long term.

WHAT UNIQUE QUALITIES DO YOU BRING TO YOUR ROLE?

We are regarded in the community as sellers agents. We acknowledge who engages us and we try to achieve the highest sale price we can while also considering their requirements.

WHAT IS YOUR DREAM HOME?

I am a big fan of the architecture of Marcio Kogan and Frank Lloyd Wright. Bayden Goddard has done a lot of homes that would meet that style on the Gold Coast and I have sold a few of them. My dream home hasn’t been built yet.

INTRO: J umping castles, pony rides, chef stations “and the whole catastrophe” as owner Mehdi Qerim puts it, have taken their place in the remarkably spacious and functional backyard of this historic Hawthorn home on a hill.
TEXT:
J umping castles, pony rides, chef stations “and the whole catastrophe” as owner Mehdi Qerim puts it, have taken their place in the remarkably spacious and functional backyard of this historic Hawthorn home on a hill.

“We’ve had epic children’s parties,” he says. “My wife Colleen is a very big believer in surrounding herself with kids. She loves kids. Lots of kids’ parties, not one for ourselves.”

There have been plenty of informal adult gatherings though, both on the huge, historic first floor westerly facing part of the wraparound verandah with sweeping city views, and in the back garden, developed meticulously by Green Aesthetics.

“Adults can sit at the table and watch the kids in the pool. It’s been a great place for our friends,” says Qerim.

Managing director of creative services agency, Yoke, Qerim says he and Colleen were looking for a home to buy when they came across the work of project manager and designer, Lee Harper, on a property they ended up not purchasing.

But once they found their property, they called upon Lee Harper Design. “Now we are great friends,” says Qerim.

Together, they honoured the 1866-built property Stanmore while contemporising it.

“He has an appreciation for timelessness, as do we,” says Qerim. “There are so many original features in the house alongside modern living.”

There were no extensions, but the interior was opened up to allow children Jonquil, 9, Dahli, 6, and Elijah, 3, “ to run full tilt and not run into anything". "There are big family spaces that they can run around in without hitting a wall.”

There’s also a secure children’s play area to the side of the house with a raised cubby house.

But it’s the kitchen with Miele appliances and a seven-metre Carrara marble bench, transformed from an area that was once a passage way that all the family really loves.

JULIETTA JAMESON

INTRO: T here would be little point buying a top penthouse in any Australian capital city if the balconies were only big enough for a quick glass of champagne.
TEXT:
T here would be little point buying a top penthouse in any Australian capital city if the balconies were only big enough for a quick glass of champagne.

“No, in the prestige market, apartment residents want their outdoor space designed around the events that are going to happen there,” says Mladen Prnjatovic of Opera Residences architects Tzannes, the latest “must buy into” Sydney harbourside apartment block, which this month saw its penthouse take out a record Australian apartment price.

“That means dining outside and without the mozzies at night you’d get in a garden of a house, having a barbecue, sitting outside, standing outside admiring the view. That external space is incredibly important, and being increasingly recognised as such.”

For Australians downsizing, who make up a large slice of the market for high-end apartments, those al fresco areas are critical. For many it’s an enduring connection to the large gardens they used to have, Prnjatovic believes. Buyers born overseas similarly see outdoor living as an essential aspect of the Australian way of life.

“At one time, people all used to congregate in the kitchen,” says Scott van den Boogaard of landscape architects ASPECT Studios. “Now they congregate more and more in outdoor spaces.

“They’re more important, particularly if there are views when they can use them almost to show off. If they have an apartment with beautiful views, access to the sunlight and a good aspect, then it’s a case of, ‘Let’s go outside and enjoy them’.”

It’s for exactly this reason that the penthouse on our cover, now for sale in a brand new apartment building in Melbourne's South Yarra, is so popular. Many of the potential buyers of the Milsons Point apartment in Sydney, also featured (opposite), say its greatest attraction is the 120 square metres of outdoor space looking straight on to the Harbour Bridge. Meanwhile the new record-breaking Opera Residences penthouse, which sold for $27 million, has a 14-square-metre wintergarden.

“It’s wonderful to have a generous outdoor area that doesn’t need all the upkeep of a large garden but which also has stunning views of the city,” says Marshall White sales executive Nicole French,  one of the agents for the South Yarra property. “Downsizers in particular love the views, and then looking at all the lights at night.”

LJ Hooker’s David Malouf, who is selling the Milsons Point apartment, says Asian buyers absolutely adore the idea of outside living too. “We’ve taken this apartment to China and they’re going, ‘Wow! That’s wonderful!’,” he says.

With external areas now used increasingly as an extension to the internal layout, the transition between the two is becoming critically important. Architect William Smart of Smart Design Studio, speaking from Berlin where he was presenting at the World Architecture Festival, says being in Europe reminds him how much the Australian climate favours outdoor living.

“Developers are now very keen to integrate these areas into apartments and for me the most important considerations are orientation, solar access and views, and to make sure it’s useable space,” he says.

“Australians have now embraced apartment living and with so many having families and pets, they want space outdoors too.”

Many also want to grow edible gardens on their balconies or terraces, says van den Boorgaard, with herbs, vegetables or lemon trees. It’s fashionable now too to make a feature of decorative pots. “We also have clients who like green walls or green balustrades which also helps to cool apartments and give a beautiful green aspect.”

Ascot

It’s hard to go past the panoramic Brisbane River and CBD skyline views but for car enthusiasts, the impressive 10-car garage deserves a mention. Agent Dwight Ferguson says approaching via the 40-metre tunnel bored into the hillside is like entering the bat cave. The home also boasts the best technology you can get. “It’s one of the better-appointed homes I’ve been into,” he says. “The house is big and modern with so many different living spaces and completely self-contained accommodation.” It’s a 10-minute drive to the CBD and airport and close to elite schools. KATE FARRELLY
